title: The Global Polycrisis
subtitle: A Comprehensive Analysis of Interconnected Global Threats, Compounding Crises, Human Exposure, Systemic Vulnerability, and Long-Term Civilizational Risk
dek: A 107-page systems synthesis of how climate change, pollution, poverty, food and water insecurity, biodiversity loss, conflict, disease, debt, education deficits and demographic change compound one another, who is exposed, how long the consequences persist, and why 2025–2050 is the decisive window for prevention.
abstract: This report examines the global polycrisis as one interconnected system rather than a list of separate problems. Climate change, pollution, poverty, food and water insecurity, biodiversity loss, conflict, disease, debt, education deficits and demographic change are treated as components that alter the conditions under which every other component develops. Its central question is how interconnected global crises reinforce one another, increase human exposure to systemic threats, and could produce enduring conditions of vulnerability over centuries to millennia. It separates established findings, conditional projections and speculative scenarios, and labels each exhibit accordingly.

The evidence reviewed supports five conclusions: hazards are rising (warming of about 1.55°C in 2024, a remaining 1.5°C carbon budget of roughly three years of current emissions, and current policies pointing to about 2.8°C by 2100); the burdens that amplify hazards remain vast (about 811 million people below the US$3-a-day line, some 645 million hungry, about 2 billion without clean cooking and about 7.9 million deaths a year linked to air pollution); these burdens are geographically concentrated where nearly all population growth this century will occur, with Africa's population projected to rise from about 1.55 billion in 2025 to 3.81 billion in 2100; the crises are causally entangled through six reinforcing loops and eight interlocking traps; and many consequences, from carbon dioxide and sea-level rise to extinction and persistent chemicals, act over centuries or longer.

The report ranks threats on eight criteria, assesses regions, and compares four stylised scenarios. It judges uneven muddling through the most likely single scenario and chronic deterioration the principal downside risk, and treats a full 'polycrisis apocalypse' (cascading, multi-regional, self-sustaining breakdown) as a low-probability tail that cannot be excluded; the scenarios are conceptual and carry no numerical probability. It identifies 2025–2050 as the decisive window for prevention. Part VII, kept separate from the diagnosis so that readers can assess the evidence independently, sets out Polycrisis Resilience, a concept presented as developed by Hunter Hughes, and the H Heuristics framework, using the Century Pathways benchmark of 859, 255 and 112 billion person-years without five basic services over 2026–2100 under frozen, trend and proven-peer-pace paths.
findings: Interaction is the defining feature of the polycrisis: a flood that meets a debt crisis, a heatwave that meets a weak grid or a drought that meets a civil war produces losses far larger than the hazard alone. The report notes that the literature now broadly agrees on a definition but still studies interactions less than single crises.
Vulnerability, not hazard, explains most of the human toll: disaster death rates have fallen by about 98% since the 1920s as societies became richer and better protected, even as hazards intensified.

On eight criteria, climate destabilisation (38 of 40) ranks first, followed by biodiversity and ecosystem loss, poverty and structural vulnerability, conflict, pollution and education deficits, because they amplify every other crisis. The report notes that the highest-ranked threats are not those with the largest annual death tolls, and that the ratings are qualitative judgements on a 1–5 scale, not statistically validated rankings.

Exposure is being redistributed toward risk through population growth, urbanisation into floodplains and informal settlements, and climate-driven displacement. About 9% of humanity already lives outside the historical human climate niche, and at about 2.7°C this could reach about one in five.

Rich countries face a different polycrisis of narrowing capacity: ageing, fiscal strain, polarisation, energy dependence and supply-chain exposure. Weighing claims about Western decline against the evidence, the report supports a 'weak' account of relative decline and stress, and finds no support for the claims that immigration is economically ruinous or that immigration or ethnic mixing causes civilisational collapse, citing population-genetics and ancient-DNA research and the US National Academies' review of immigration's economic and fiscal effects.

Chronic deterioration is judged more likely than sudden global collapse. Of four stylised scenarios (accelerated resilience, uneven muddling through, chronic deterioration and polycrisis apocalypse), uneven muddling through is judged the most likely single scenario and chronic deterioration the main downside risk; a polycrisis apocalypse is low-probability but not negligible. The report lists monitorable signposts, each of which policy can influence.

The window is 2025–2050: the 1.5°C carbon budget, the build-out of African and South Asian cities, the schooling of today's children and the refinancing of developing-country debt all fall in this period, and choices made inside it are cheap relative to those made after. Prevention in early warning, resilient infrastructure, clean energy, clean cooking, education and health is reported to return several dollars per dollar and cut several vulnerabilities at once.

The response, Polycrisis Resilience, is set out in a separate part so the diagnosis can be judged on its own. It aims to reduce human and systemic vulnerability through eight domains of action, and uses the Century Pathways benchmark: a gap of about 143 billion person-years without five basic services between current trend and proven peer pace over 2026–2100.
method: A structured synthesis of IPCC, UN agency and World Bank assessment reports, peer-reviewed literature on polycrisis, systemic risk, compound events, tipping points, poverty traps, conflict, health and demography, and the H Heuristics research series, cited to the latest editions available in November 2026. Charts of temperature, population, fertility, disaster mortality and solar prices use public HadCRUT5, UN World Population Prospects 2024, EM-DAT and Our World in Data series processed by H Heuristics. The system map, threat and regional ratings (on a 1–5 scale against stated criteria) and the four scenarios are the author's constructions; the report states that the ratings are meant to structure discussion rather than provide statistically validated rankings and that the scenario trajectories are conceptual and carry no numerical probability. Each exhibit is labelled as an established finding, a conditional projection or a speculative scenario, and outlooks beyond 2100 are treated as speculative. Where H Heuristics publications differ, the report follows the November 2026 Update (HH-2026-64). It contains 18 figures and 31 tables across thirty-three sections in eight parts, with a methods appendix and glossary.
